metadata.note: ai-explainer / claude-hai. AI Debt Tracker WEEK 4. ILLUSTRATE LAW: the Claude UI appears at B00 (cold open, answered), B09 (verdict artifact), B10 (handoff) and B11 (outro) only — every body beat illustrates its concept as a native animated Remotion scene (REBUILD LAW). The four source PNGs and their SVG sources are REFERENCE in pantry/, never slotted as media. The script's five body sections become eight body beats: 0:15 splits into the pipeline (B01) and the worked copy check (B02); 0:45 splits into the bake-off (B03) and what pointing actually buys (B04); 1:20's tally becomes B05; and the closing on-camera section becomes a limits beat. FIVE THINGS NOT TO GET WRONG: the reader is NOT more accurate — B2 read every field right and the reel says so on four separate frames; the three bars do not share a denominator; the reader invents more instruments than either baseline; the fresh triage check FAILED; and the week's gate records DELEGATED, not cleared — no person has reviewed any of it. VERTICAL CUT: every beat re-renders from a <pattern>916 portrait composition — a re-layout, never a crop. The narration mp3s are copied from the 16:9 reel, not regenerated, so the two masters are the same edit.

beats.narration_text: Hi, I'm Om Mali. This video is about teaching my A I debt tracker to read a debt announcement into structured facts, where every number points back to the sentence it came from. This is week four of the A I Debt Tracker. It passed the check it was set. A simpler baseline still read more fields right.

shot.visual_intent: COLD OPEN LAW: the ask is the week itself. It lands ANSWERED, and the answer contains its own bad news — the pass and the baseline that beat it are on the same frame from the first beat.

props.command: Read every debt filing into structured bonds and loans. The model never types a number — it points at the words it read, and code parses them. Then show me what the pointing actually bought.

beats.narration_text: Last week the agent learned to find the debt news. This week it reads it. The rule from week one is that the model never types a number. So the reader works in three steps. Code picks the passages that state debt terms. The model lists each bond and copies the exact words for every value, naming the passage. Then code checks those words are really there, and parses the number.

shot.visual_intent: A list of three steps STATES the rule. A code-model-code sandwich, with the model as the only accented card, shows it.

show.at: on 'the model never types a number'
show.event: The rule lands above the three steps.
Code, then the model in the accent, then code again.

beats.narration_text: And that check earned its place. For Alphabet's euro bonds, the model said it copied one and a half billion dollars. The filing says euros. It rewrote the currency sign while claiming to copy. Those words aren't in the passage, so the values were refused — missing, rather than wrong. That is the trade the design asked for.

shot.visual_intent: One character is the whole beat, so one character is what the frame marks. The € in the filing and the $ in the copy are the only highlighted things on screen.

The dollar copy lights beneath it — one character apart.

beats.narration_text: I tested it on twenty-four filings whose sixty-six bonds and loans were labelled before anything ran. The week's check was simple: beat plain pattern matching. It did — ninety-four percent of fields right against eighty-four. The denominators differ, and the reader reported twenty-nine instruments the filings never announce. But the third bar is the honest one. Asking the same model to type the numbers got every field right.

shot.visual_intent: Three bars, three different denominators, each printed. The extras sit past a divider on their OWN scale because they count instruments and the bars count fields.

props.verdict: The week 4 check, fixed in the design in week 1, was to beat B1. The reader did: 157 of 167 fields against 135 of 160. But B2 read 160 of 160.

beats.narration_text: So what did pointing buy? Not accuracy. On clean pricing documents a small model reads numbers well. What the reader adds is a sentence behind every value — an id you can open and read. And it fails safe: when the model writes a number that isn't in the filing, the number is refused instead of used.

shot.visual_intent: The honest comparison drawn as two cards. The left one is CORRECT; the point is that it cannot be audited. Nothing on this frame says the reader is more accurate, because it is not.

beats.narration_text: Across the set, two hundred and twenty-seven copied values were found in the passage the model cited. Three turned up in a different passage. Twenty-four were refused. Eight of those were currency signs rewritten, like Alphabet's. The other sixteen were the model writing the word null — bookkeeping, with no effect on any score.

beats.narration_text: I also re-checked last week's triage on fifty new filings, labelled first. It found eight of nine — below my ninety-five percent line. That is a failed check and I am not dressing it up. The miss was an I B M prospectus whose cover leaves even the year blank. I logged it and didn't tune it away. Nine positives is a small check, and I say so.

beats.narration_text: The limits. Ninety-four percent is on twenty-four filings that are mostly clean pricing documents — sixty-two of the sixty-six instruments were new notes. The labels are Claude's reading, machine-checked but not read by a person. And the week's gate says delegated, not cleared: I handed the whole week to Claude and have not reviewed any of it. Next week connects the reader to a ledger.

beats.narration_text: So: an event reader where code picks the passages, the model points at words, and code parses the numbers. Ninety-four percent of fields right against eighty-four for regex rules — it passes. One model call typing the values read all of them. Twenty-four copies refused, eight of them rewritten currency signs. Fresh triage failed at eight of nine, the answer key agreed on one of five, and nobody has reviewed any of it.

shot.visual_intent: Judgment beat. The artifact page is the point (ILLUSTRATE LAW carve-out). Two of the five findings are failures, and they are not last.

show.event: Five findings stagger in, one per spoken clause.

props.artifactTitle: Reading Debt Announcements into Cited Facts
props.artifactHeading: What week 4 built, and what it is allowed to claim
artifactLines: An event reader in three steps: code picks the passages that state debt terms, the model lists each instrument and copies the exact words for every value, and code checks the words are really there before parsing the number. The model never types a number.
On 24 filings whose 66 instruments were labelled before any run, it read 157 of 167 fields right (94%) against 135 of 160 (84%) for regex rules. That was the week's check, and it passes.

B2 one model call — the model typing every value itself — read 160 of 160. The reader's gain is a cited sentence behind every value, not accuracy. It also reported 29 instruments the filings do not announce, against 9 and 1.
The copy check refused 24 of 254 copied values: 8 were currency signs the model rewrote while claiming to copy, 16 were the word "null". A refused value is missing, not wrong.
Fresh triage found 8 of 9 — below the 95% line, logged as P46 and not tuned away. The answer key agreed on 1 of 5 fresh reports with 4 new defects. The gate records the week DELEGATED, not CLEARED.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude. Before you build the clever version, run the stupid one. Mine beat the baseline it was measured against and lost to the one it wasn't. If your system is more complicated, be able to say what the complication buys.

shot.visual_intent: HANDOFF LAW: a real prompt, read ALOUD verbatim and then discussed. One of exactly two typing beats. It is the lesson of this week turned into something a viewer can run.

show.event: The prompt types into the composer.

props.segment: Reading Debt Announcements into Cited Facts
props.command: Before I build the structured, grounded version of this, write and run the dumbest baseline that could possibly work — one call, no scaffolding. Score both on the same labelled set and show me the denominators. Then tell me in one sentence what my complicated version buys that the simple one does not, and if the answer is "nothing I measured", say that instead.
